name: Tara Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at a farm machinery dealer just outside the market town. Tractors, balers, mowers, that sort of thing. I book the service jobs for the three mechanics, chase the parts orders, file the warranty claims and do the paperwork when a machine's sold. I've been there just over a year, and I'm still learning the warranty side, the manufacturers' forms are a nightmare.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who are the people you deal with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly farmers, and they ring at six in the morning when a baler's broken in the middle of silage. You learn to talk fast and book them in before they lose their temper. My partner Callum works on his family's dairy farm, so I know what a broken machine in June means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was overblown. At the dealership the lads would have a laugh about it. I might mention it at the young farmers' social, but I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, which suits me. Farmers want a person on the phone who knows the difference between a baler and a mower. The only thing I think about is whether the dealership keeps going, because two others in the county have shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on, and I'd keep using the AI thing now and then for warranty letters, because the boss showed us and it helps with the wording. I'd keep saving, we've got about three months between us. And I'd keep helping out on Callum's farm at weekends, because that's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two dealerships have shut. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The big manufacturers are pushing farmers to buy online and go to the main dealers in the city. If ours closed, I'd have to drive forty minutes for an office job, or work on the farm full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would working on the farm full-time mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less money, more hours. Callum's dad pays family in milk and beef, not wages. We'd never go hungry on the farm, and I'd be doing something real.

say: I'd say I always thought AI was **overblown**.
I might mention it at the **young farmers' social**, but I wouldn't post about it.
think: Farmers want a **person on the phone** who knows their machines.
My worry is the **dealership closing**, since two in the county have shut.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for warranty letters, as the boss showed us.
Keep saving our **three months** and help on Callum's farm at weekends.
S0.quote: We'd never go hungry on the farm, and I'd be doing something real.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure** because farmers want a human voice.
Her real worry is the **dealership closing** as others have.
The **family farm** is a fallback, paid in food rather than wages.

steps.text: Draft warranty letters with the AI tool now and then
Help on Callum's family dairy farm every weekend
Keep adding to the three months of shared savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers will always want a person, so dealers will be all right. I'd tell the lads to learn the new booking system. I'd say it's progress, like when tractors got computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, booking, ordering parts, warranty forms, that's my job, and it's all on your list. If the manufacturer's software does the warranty claims and the parts orders automatically, there's not much left for me. The mechanics are safe, though, robots aren't fixing balers in a field any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system as soon as the boss had it, because once others have tried it I pick it up fine. I'd ask about moving onto the parts counter, which is more hands-on, knowing the parts and dealing with farmers. And I'd keep the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened. There's time in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really. It's business. If the software's cheaper, the boss has to use it, he's got his own bills. I'd rather adapt than moan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Callum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come and work on the farm, and he'd half mean it. His family would have me. But I'd want my own wage, I don't want to be paid in milk.

say: I'd say farmers will always want a **person**, so dealers will be fine.
I'd call it **progress**, like when tractors got computers.
think: Booking, parts and **warranty forms** are all on the list.
The **mechanics** are safe, because robots aren't fixing balers in fields.
do: Learn the **new system** as soon as the boss brings it in.
Ask to move onto the **parts counter**, which is more hands-on.
S1.quote: I'd want my own wage, I don't want to be paid in milk.
fieldNote: She **blames no one**, seeing it as normal business.
Her plan is the **parts counter**, a more hands-on role.
Values **independence**: her own wage, not family payment.

steps.text: Learn the dealership's new booking system
Ask to move onto the parts counter
Keep three months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and too fast. At the social I'd say we need to look after our own. I'm not one for government handouts, but people will need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm done in the office by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can do the bookings and warranty forms. The parts counter might last until the robots come, but that's 2031, three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the parts counter straight away. I'd talk to Callum about the farm, maybe I'd take over the books and the milk records there, but that's thinking work too. We'd stop saving for a house and keep the money in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach's in knots thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm's books are thinking work too. So what's left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calving, milking, the hands-on stuff, until the robots come for that too. I grew up in town, I'm not a natural with cows. But I'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say come home. Callum's family would say stay on the farm. I'd want to stand on my own feet, but I'd probably need them.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and too fast.
I'd say we need to **look after our own**, not rely on handouts.
think: I'm **done in the office** by 2028, because bookings and warranty forms are thinking work.
The **parts counter** might last until robots arrive in 2031.
do: Ask for the **parts counter** job straight away.
Talk with Callum about **farm work**, including calving and milking.
Stop saving for a **house** and keep the money in case.
S2.quote: I grew up in town, I'm not a natural with cows. But I'd learn.
fieldNote: She sees office work go first and **hands-on work** later.
Her fallback is **Callum's farm**, but she wants independence.

steps.text: Ask the boss for the parts counter job
Learn calving and milking on Callum's farm
Stop saving for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it instead of moaning. I'd tell the lads at the dealership to learn the new systems while the old ones still run. It's a big change, but people round here have managed big changes before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to move into parts and learn the farm properly. I'd be thirty-two when the office side goes, which is young enough to start again. It's the robots in 2034 that bother me, because that's when the farm and the parts counter get hit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the parts counter within a year or two, and learn the part numbers for every baler we sell. I'd spend Saturdays on Callum's farm learning milking and the calving pens, properly this time. I'd keep our savings at three months and push the house back until we see how the dealership holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got a plan, and that helps. It's the not knowing what comes after 2034 that sits in my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan for 2034, when robots can do the hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd hope the farm still needs a person to keep an eye on things, even if a robot does the milking. Callum's uncle already has a milking robot, and he still gets up at five to check on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans with Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably we'd marry sooner, next year rather than in three. I'd want us settled and on the same page before things get rough. His mum would be thrilled, she's been asking for two years.

say: I'd say we've **got time**, so use it.
I'd tell the lads at the dealership to **learn** the new systems while there's time.
think: Five years gives me time to move into **parts** and the farm.
do: Move to the **parts counter** within a year or two.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to move into parts and learn the farm properly.
fieldNote: She uses extra time to **step** from office to parts to farm.
Unsure about **2034**, she hopes to run robots.

steps.text: Move to the parts counter within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and farmers have seen worse than this. My granddad lived through the switch from horses to tractors and he was fine. I'd tell people not to get worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels all right. I'd have time to move to parts, learn the farm properly, and maybe buy a bit of land with Callum. I'd be thirty-seven when it comes, settled, with a trade in my hands as well as the office stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the parts counter in two or three years, once the new systems have settled in the office. We'd get married in the next couple of years and buy a small house near the farm, because land round there only goes up. And I'd keep learning the dairy side at weekends, milking and calving, so I'm useful there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a long road, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once the others at work had. I'm never the first to try a new thing, but I'm never the last either. If the boss uses it for parts orders and it works, I'll use it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work, one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to work with your hands, and stay close to family. A screen job can be taken off you in a year. A farm and a family take a lot longer to lose.

I'd point to my **granddad**, who lived through horses giving way to tractors.

Her advice to future children centres on **hands and family**, not screens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My office job goes fast and I'd be relying on Callum's family. What would help is the dealership training people for parts and repairs, and family close by.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much family matters. When things go wrong, it's family that catches you, not the government.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, it's family that catches you, not the government.
portrait: Tara runs the **office** at a farm machinery dealer in a market town.
She's **traditional**, values **family**, and picks up technology once others have.
Her partner Callum works on his family's **dairy farm**, her fallback in hard times.
She plans to move to the **parts counter**, then farm work, as AI spreads.
She wants her **own wage**, not to be paid in milk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her office job goes and she'd depend on family.
whatWouldHelp: **Training** for parts and repairs, and **family** close by.
